section_name: Script 1 — Don't Just Teach the Skill — Reveal the Secret Behind It
content:
Script 1 — Don't Just Teach the Skill — Reveal the Secret Behind It

Here's a powerful shift in thinking: Don't just teach a skill — reveal the secret behind it. Definitions, examples, anchor charts... those tell students WHAT a skill is. And "knowing what" is important — but it's not the secret to mastery.

Mastery comes from knowing HOW to EXECUTE the skill. And the truth is, students don't gain know-how from WATCHING us do the work. They gain it when we reveal what's-going-on-in-our-heads WHILE we're doing work.

Students don't naturally possess the thinking that develops reading and writing skills. Those mental moves aren't instinctual. They're invisible. That's WHY we need to teach explicitly and with clarity.

When modeling a new skill to readers or writers, we must divulge our thinking... disclose our reasoning... unveil the mental moves. Teaching explicitly requires describing the parts of the skill that they can't see — the decision making process.

As identified by John Hattie within his meta-analysis research: Explicit teaching — the ability to clearly reveal how a skill works — is one of the most significant influencers on improving student learning.

So tomorrow, choose a skill your students are struggling with — Then, plan exactly what you'll reveal during your demonstration: what you'll notice... what you'll question... what you'll adjust... and what you'll decide. Leave nothing to mystery. Let them in on the secret.
skill_title: Don't Just Teach the Skill — Reveal the Secret Behind It

section_name: Script 2 — Think-Alouds Look Spontaneous... But They're Not
content:
Script 2 — Think-Alouds Look Spontaneous... But They're Not

Let me clear up a myth that gets teachers into trouble: You don't wing a think-aloud. And if you try... it shows.

Here's why. We, as skilled readers and writers, know how to execute the skill. We know how to insert an appropriate transition. We know how to determine the main idea. We know how to use context clues to figure out an unfamiliar word. We do these skills every day. But we do them automatically. We know how to do these skills. But we don't always know HOW we know how to do these skills — and THAT's the problem.

Within a mini-lesson, we are not merely teaching WHAT the skill is. We are teaching HOW to do it. That means BEFORE the lesson, we have to execute the skill ourselves — slowly, deliberately, thoughtfully — all so that WE can notice the tiny decisions that WE make along the way. BEFORE the lesson, we have to recognize and identify each step in the journey of our thinking in order to reveal it to our students.

If we don't do this ahead of time... If we just jump in and try to "wing a Think Aloud"... we tend to generalize the thinking process, speak broadly and vaguely about our thoughts, or omit them entirely.

Here's the irony: A great think-aloud APPEARS spontaneous... But it is 100% rehearsed. It's you REPEATING the thinking process that you originally executed when you were PLANNING this lesson example.
skill_title: Think-Alouds Look Spontaneous... But They're Not

section_name: Script 2 — Think-Alouds Look Spontaneous... But They're Not (continued)
content:
Script 2 (continued) — Benefits of Planning a Think-Aloud

When we've thought through the thinking ahead of time:
- We know exactly what we want students to hear.
- We know the exact moment we want to emphasize.
- We know the text detail that triggers confusion.
- We know the decision that moves the skill forward.
- We know the exact words we'll use to make our thinking visible.

That planned think-aloud is like a rehearsal. It frees us to act naturally DURING the mini-lesson model. Now that I know everything I want to SAY, I can lean in... pause... struggle a little... sound authentic... all without losing clarity and focus on the MINI skill I'm modeling.

So tomorrow, BEFORE your next mini-lesson, execute the example yourself — slowly. Consciously think through each step. Take note of what you saw... thought... and decided... Notice the micro-decisions you made and the order you made them in... because THIS is what you want to repeat DURING the mini-lesson.

Ironically, a think-aloud shouldn't be made up in the moment — It should just LOOK like it is.
skill_title: Think-Alouds Look Spontaneous... But They're Not (continued)

section_name: Script 3 — Think-Aloud Questions Aren't for Students. They're for You.
content:
Script 3 — Think-Aloud Questions Aren't for Students. They're for You.

All questions asked during a Think Aloud are rhetorical. We aren't asking students to answer them. In fact, the questions voiced during a Think Aloud aren't for the kids at all — They're for you, the teacher, to answer yourself.

A think-aloud is not a quiz. It's not a comprehension check. It's not an invitation for students to answer. A think-aloud includes YOU asking yourself questions — and then YOU wrestling your way toward the answer out loud. It's rhetorical. It's reflective. It's metacognitive.

Rhetorical questions asked within a Think Aloud sound like this:
- "What does the author mean here?"
- "What's going on in this part?"
- "How can I figure this out?"
- "How can I do that in my writing?"
- "What could I do to make that better?"

These ARE questions that YOU will pose in a Think Aloud — but they are followed with YOU answering them yourself. They're spoken publicly so students can hear the mental moves and intentional choices that make the skill work.

When the teacher recognizes that Think Aloud questions are asked of herself... and we stop expecting students to answer them... Then we stop pulling kids into cognitive work they aren't ready for. This is Step 2 of the 4-step mini-lesson. This is when I-DO-the-work and students watch & listen.
skill_title: Think-Aloud Questions Aren't for Students. They're for You.

section_name: Script 3 — Think-Aloud Questions Aren't for Students. They're for You. (continued)
content:
Script 3 (continued) — The Language of a Think-Aloud Is Personal

By asking rhetorical questions, we stay in teaching mode. We slow down the model. We think deliberately. We share the mental work that skilled readers and writers do.

The language of a think-aloud is personal. It's full of I, me, and my statements.
- "I think the next step is to..."
- "I see this detail, and I think..."
- "I remember earlier when the author..."

And because it's real thinking, it's naturally messy: Full of fragments... stops and starts... "wait..." ... "hold on..." ... "let me rethink this..." That's what makes it authentic. That's what makes it teachable.

Tomorrow, during your next mini-lesson, stop yourself before you ask students a question in the I DO... Rather, redirect that question inward...
- "What am I thinking...?"
- "What does my mind do when I'm stuck?"
- "What would I try next?"

ASK these questions of yourself... And then ANSWER them yourself. Because in a real think-aloud, the questions aren't for the students — they're for the teacher.
skill_title: Think-Aloud Questions Aren't for Students. They're for You. (continued)

section_name: Script 4 — Don't Make It Look Easy — Model the Struggle
content:
Script 4 — "Don't Make It Look Easy — Model the Struggle."

If we want students to truly learn how to execute a reading or writing skill, then we need to provide more than a polished example. They need to be privy to the behind-the-curtain thinking.

When we demonstrate a skill within a mini-lesson, we tend to clean it up. We smooth it out. We show how to do it in neat, tidy, perfect steps. And in the process, we make it look efficient... automatic... and easy. But that's not how REAL readers or writers operate.

Real thinking is messy. It stops. It starts. It backtracks. It fragments. It gets stuck. It tries something... then tries something else. And students need to SEE THAT!

Because when we make reading and writing look effortless, students assume:
- "It's supposed to be easy."
- "If I struggle, I must be doing it wrong."
- "Good readers don't get confused."
- "Good writers don't change their minds."
But none of that is true!

During the I-DO-of-a-mini-lesson, students need to be privy to the real stuff: the frustrations, the adjustments, the authentic problem-solving that experts do.
skill_title: Don't Make It Look Easy — Model the Struggle

section_name: Script 4 — Don't Make It Look Easy — Model the Struggle (continued)
content:
Script 4 (continued) — How to Model the Struggle in a Think-Aloud

Students need to hear the thinking of a LESS-confident reader or writer:
- "Hmm... I don't get this part... Maybe I should reread."
- "This doesn't sound right... What's a different detail I could try..."
- "Aghhh... That's still not working... Maybe I could try this instead..."

These thoughts aren't mistakes. They're the very cognitive moves that make a skill possible. The key to a powerful Think Aloud is: Don't hide the struggle. Talk through it! Model your journey of thinking — the entire, unvarnished, IMperfect journey of thinking.

This allows you to show your readers and writers what it looks like to persevere. To grit through confusion. To troubleshoot meaning. To wrestle with a sentence until it makes sense. To revise thinking because new information changes your understanding.

Students don't naturally learn this. It's not intuitive. They don't magically "pick up" this mental work. They become skilled when we open the curtain and let them see what's usually invisible.

Tomorrow, when you plan your lesson model, identify a common struggle point students have and then... show the authentic struggle: a place you reread... a decision you reconsider... a moment something doesn't sound right... a place you try again. Let students be privy to the real thinking — the human thinking — the thinking that makes the skill work.

Because the goal isn't to make reading and writing look easy. The goal is to make the thinking visible.
skill_title: Don't Make It Look Easy — Model the Struggle (continued)

section_name: Script 5 — Knowing WHAT and Knowing HOW Are Not the Same Thing
content:
Script 5 — Knowing WHAT and Knowing HOW Are Not the Same Thing

Here's a truth that can transform explicit instruction: Telling students WHAT a skill is... is not the same as teaching them HOW to do it.

We tell students WHAT all day long.
- What is a topic sentence
- What is a main idea
- What good writers do

And during these lessons, we introduce a new skill — and students can repeat it back. We show examples of the skill, and they nod along. And when the lesson ends, we assume they're ready to practice the skill on their own. And yet — they can't.

Here's the disconnect: If we only tell students WHAT to do, we can't expect them to know HOW to do it. When students can define a skill... but struggle to apply it independently... we often assume they don't know what to do. And yet, they know exactly what they're supposed to do — they just don't know how to get there.

This is the difference between model the noun and model the verb. When we show a finished example, that's SHOWING-a-model — the noun. We reveal the product, the outcome, the goal — so students can see what the skill looks like. This is an important element in teaching a new skill. However, it doesn't mean they can execute it.
skill_title: Knowing WHAT and Knowing HOW Are Not the Same Thing

section_name: Script 5 — Knowing WHAT and Knowing HOW Are Not the Same Thing (continued)
content:
Script 5 (continued) — Modeling the Verb: Execution Over Definition

Execution requires modeling — the verb. After telling students about the skill, we must execute it live and in front of them. Without this active demonstration, students know the destination — but not the path.

They may know the language of the skill. And the purpose it serves. But they haven't seen the thinking that makes the skill work.

Modeling the verb includes:
- performing the actions
- making the decisions
- and voicing the mental moves that produce the result

When students "aren't getting it," it's rarely because they don't know WHAT the teacher wants or WHAT they should be doing. More often, it's that they don't know HOW to do it.

Knowledge alone isn't enough... Students need access to the know-how, too.
skill_title: Knowing WHAT and Knowing HOW Are Not the Same Thing (continued)

section_name: Script 6 — When I'm Thinking Aloud... YOU Have a Job Too
content:
Script 6 — When I'm Thinking Aloud... YOU Have a Job Too

Students play a key role during explicit instruction: While I DO an example... The students are to watch & listen. But often, a couple eager students jump in and start helping the teacher during the model... and we, the teachers, often let them.

Here's the disconnect: The I DO is the teacher-only part of the lesson. It's a monologue — not a dialogue. The I DO is where the teacher shows HER thinking, HER process, HER struggle. The students' job is to watch & listen, to follow the teacher's thinking, to listen carefully as the teacher navigates the skill, to pay attention to the decisions that make the skill work.

When students jump in and start helping us execute the I DO, we often interpret that as readiness... "If students can help, then they're ready to do it on their own." But that's a mistake. The teacher's model isn't for the students who can help. It's for the students who can't.

When a few students jump in during the I DO, it creates a false sense of readiness. It interrupts the model for the students who still need to see the thinking unfold.

To encourage engagement — but keep students from helping you — provide them a way to communicate that they're "getting it"... that they're tracking your thinking — WITHOUT TALKING.
- A subtle nod.
- A simple thumbs-up while you're modeling.
- A hand signal that says, I'm thinking like you.

These are all evidence of student engagement WITHOUT interrupting the flow of the I DO.

Tomorrow, before you teach your next mini-lesson, take a moment to clarify the purpose of the I DO... and the students' job during it... Because, yes, they do play a role... it's just not the one they think it is.
skill_title: When I'm Thinking Aloud... YOU Have a Job Too

section_name: Script 7 — They Can't Follow Your Thinking If They Can't See the Text
content:
Script 7 — They Can't Follow Your Thinking If They Can't See the Text

When it comes to modeling a new skill, here's something teachers don't always consider: Students can't follow your thinking if they can't see what you're thinking about.

During a think-aloud, students must be able to see the text — whether it's what you're reading or what you're writing. They need to see what your eyes are on. They need to distinguish between what you're reading and what you're thinking... between what you're writing and what you're thinking. And none of that works if students can't clearly see the text itself. If they can't see the text, they can't follow the thinking.

They need to see the exact sentence you're revising. The specific detail you're reacting to as a reader. The phrase that's confusing you. The paragraph you're reorganizing.

Students need a clear, shared view of the text you're thinking about.
- That means the passage can't be on a loose handout.
- It can't be in a book you're holding up.
- And it can't be a textbook everyone is looking at individually.

If students aren't looking at both you and the text you're thinking about, you can't control what they're seeing. Consequently, the text needs to be big and public.
- Projected.
- Written on the board.
- Or revealed on chart paper.

Students need to see your finger move across the sentence — and stop when you are sharing a thought. They need to see when your marker pauses, when your cursor hesitates, when a word gets deleted, when something new replaces it. They need to see your thinking grow, shift, and change in real time.

SEEING is part of the learning. Seeing is part of the thinking.

Before your next explicit lesson, decide how you'll make the text visible to everyone — so students can see not just the skill... but the thinking that makes it work.
skill_title: They Can't Follow Your Thinking If They Can't See the Text

section_name: Script 8 — The Think-Aloud Powers the Gradual Release
content:
Script 8 — The Think-Aloud Powers the Gradual Release

We hear about the gradual release all the time in education. I DO. WE DO. YOU DO. It's familiar. It's logical. It's everywhere. But here's what teachers sometimes overlook: A strong I DO fuels the entire gradual release. It determines whether the rest of the sequence works.

When the I DO is explicit — when the teacher's thinking is clear, deliberate, and authentic — students know exactly what to try during the whole-class WE DO. But if the teacher's model is vague, rushed, or silent, only a handful of students participate in the WE DO.

The strength of the I DO feeds the confidence and participation in the WE DO... and together, they determine the success of the YOU DO.

The YOU DO is where students attempt the skill independently. The same skill the teacher modeled. The same thinking the class practiced together. When the I DO is strong, and students actively participated in the WE DO, they enter the YOU DO prepared, confident, and capable.

But when the I DO is weak... the WE DO often lacks participation... and the YOU DO becomes something students can't seem to do.

Although the teacher's I DO is just one part of the gradual release, it's the engine that drives the entire sequence — making the skill make sense, making it achievable, and making mastery possible.
skill_title: The Think-Aloud Powers the Gradual Release

section_name: Script 9 — Modeling and Thinking Aloud Are Not the Same
content:
Script 9 — Modeling and Thinking Aloud Are Not the Same

Here's a distinction that can completely change the delivery of your explicit instruction: Modeling an example and thinking aloud are not the same thing. Strong teaching requires both — at the same time.

A model shows students the actions of a skill. It's physical. It's concrete. It's what students can see the teacher doing. When we model, we demonstrate the visible moves like: reading an excerpt, highlighting a detail, and jotting a note. Or crossing out a weak word and replacing it with a stronger one. These are small, deliberate actions that show what to do when executing the skill.

But a model alone is incomplete. While students can see the actions — they can't see the thinking behind them. That's where the think-aloud comes in.

A think-aloud reveals the invisible work. It makes the mental process audible. It explains HOW the teacher realized WHAT to do next — and WHY. A think-aloud connects the physical actions. It's the thinking BETWEEN each step.

It's not model OR think-aloud. It's not model, THEN think-aloud. It's model WHILE thinking aloud.

Pairing the thoughts that precede the actions is what makes instruction truly explicit. Students need to watch you do the skill WHILE listening to the reasoning that makes the skill work. When the two are separated, students can't connect the action to the decision that triggered it. But when they're fused — when your finger points to a word at the same moment your voice explains what you're thinking — students learn the "whys" behind a new skill. And that's when learning sticks.

So when planning your next lesson, don't just determine what example to model — Also plan HOW you'll demonstrate it. What thinking you will reveal when executing each action. What decisions you will face. What choices you will explain... Because true explicit teaching is the fusion of the two — modeling while thinking aloud.
skill_title: Modeling and Thinking Aloud Are Not the Same
